articleTitle: Optimization of microgrid with demand side management using Genetic Algorithm
publicationTitle: IET Conference on Power in Unity: a Whole System Approach
abstract: In a smart grid environment, economic operation means not only to economic scheduling of generation, but also to scheduling the load. In a Microgrid (MG), which comprises of intermittent Distributed Generators (DGs) (eg. solar and wind energy sources), the need of Demand Side Management (DSM)/ Demand Response (DR) becomes significant. The key point in DSM is to shift the load to some other point in time, this causes inconvenience to the customer and therefore it should be minimized. Minimizing the cost of generation and also minimizing the inconvenience caused due to shifting of loads is a multiobjective optimization problem. In this work the authors consider an industrial/ commercial MG with one solar source, two diesel generators and one battery, with the assumption that the utility grid uses dynamic pricing. The objective function contains discontinuous functions which will be difficult to solve using conventional optimization techniques and hence a Genetic Algorithm (GA) based solution is proposed. The simulation results show that there is savings for the customer with DSM compared to the case without DSM.

articleTitle: Integration of wind power using V2G as a flexible storage
publicationTitle: IET Conference on Power in Unity: a Whole System Approach
abstract: Wind power is anticipated to be the dominant Renewable Energy Sources (RES) in the UK by the year 2020. It is estimated that, there will be 41 GW of operational offshore wind in the UK beyond the 2020s. This wind penetration would likely increase the excess of electricity production. In this paper the Great Britain (GB) energy system was modelled at the national level for a range of wind power penetration and three different transport scenarios; vehicles with Internal Combustion engines (IC), Electric Vehicles (EVs) without Vehicle-to-Grid (V2G) capability, and EVs with V2G capability. Two additional scenarios for the electricity sector; CHP and non-CHP were also included in the model. A scaled down system was also modelled as a Virtual Power Plant (VPP) that aggregates several microgenerators, loads and flexible storage capacities. The first model is studied in terms of Critical Excess Electricity Production (CEEP) and CO2 emissions, and the value of using EVs as flexible storage is illustrated with different levels of wind power integration. In the second study case, the necessary electricity imports for the VPP in all transport scenarios are evaluated. Adding V2G capability in EVs can provide a flexible energy storage mechanism that reduces the necessary electricity imports, and increases the autonomy of such systems, even at low wind power penetration levels.

articleTitle: Distributed energy storage using second-life electric vehicle batteries
publicationTitle: IET Conference on Power in Unity: a Whole System Approach
abstract: Future Electric Vehicle (EV) penetration scenarios predict that in the next decades, thousands of electric vehicles will appear on the UK roads. Electric vehicle batteries are no longer considered fit for purpose after certain amount of degradation, e.g. below 80% of their initial capacity. However, they can be re-purposed for other uses, including stationary electricity storage. This paper examines the future availability of end-of-life electric vehicle batteries, and their potential use as distributed energy storage. The cost of infrastructure upgrades due to the additional peak load of electric vehicles is compared with the estimated distributed energy storage installation cost.

articleTitle: The Load Management Functions that must be delivered by the Smart Metering System
publicationTitle: IET Conference on Power in Unity: a Whole System Approach
abstract: Great-Britain's unique Radio Teleswitch System (RTS) was developed in the 1970s, deployed en-masse by the Electricity Industry during the 80s and 90s. Today it controls electric storage and water-heating in homes numbering in the low millions. The need for its development mirrors the conditions of the near future, where much generating plant capacity will close and there will be a great expansion of electric heating in the form of heat-pumps. The system allowed this expansion to occur while limiting its economic impact on generation, transmission and distribution networks. This is as relevant today as it was in the past and provides functionality that the Smart Metering System (SMS) must duplicate, or else trigger network investments and higher costs for consumers.

articleTitle: Ancillary services provided by renewable energy sources
publicationTitle: IET Conference on Power in Unity: a Whole System Approach
abstract: There are many attempts to standardise and regulate quality of supply in electricity markets. The paper is focused on quality of supply improvement in distributed electricity systems operating in accordance with electricity market rules. Quality of supply can be ensured by Ancillary Services provided by power generating units including Renewable Energy Sources. Such power generating units are equipped with electronic power inverters installed in every phase of electric connections. The inverters are fully controlled and can operate as current sources providing not only reactive power but also compensating the asymmetry and harmonic distortion. The paper presents the rules for Nodal Area Operator, which by the adequate optimisation and control is able to balance electric energy and improve power quality using Ancillary Services.

articleTitle: Estimation of the limiting penetration of low carbon connections through an assessment of LV harmonics
publicationTitle: IET Conference on Power in Unity: a Whole System Approach
abstract: Delivery of the UK Government's Carbon Plan to achieve the reduction in emissions required for compliance with the fourth carbon budget will drive an increasing number of non-linear connections onto electrical distribution networks. More photo voltaic generators, heat source pumps and electric vehicle charging points are expected to increase harmonic distortion levels on the LV system. Commissioned by Electricity North West Limited, a simple assessment has been undertaken to determine the likely amount of these harmonicproducing connections to low voltage distribution networks that could be made whilst maintaining harmonic voltage distortion values below the planning levels of Engineering Recommendation G5/4-1 [3]. Using typical system parameters, harmonic voltage distortion values were estimated based on assumed current injections from the new connections and average network background harmonics, calculated from measurements at 50 random LV sites. It was found that the limiting penetration level of low carbon connections was 40% of the distribution substation rating and it is postulated that this could be extrapolated to apply to the entire UK distribution network.

articleTitle: Market-based local balancing in distribution networks
publicationTitle: IET Conference on Power in Unity: a Whole System Approach
abstract: Increasing penetration of DG and RES results from EU energy and climate policy. The first phase of DG and RES development, called produce and forget endangers power system operation and causes more and more problems within increasing number of units connected. Therefore, approach transformation from produce and forget to system responsibilities is required. The only measure, which allows for taking into account power system aspect, economics and electricity generation is optimisation implemented as a part of local balancing system. Local balancing concept proposed in the paper includes energy balancing, power flows and power losses. The paper analyses operation of distribution network with DG units and verifies results from balancing system application. Authors indicates also the future needs in the field of active management of distribution networks.

articleTitle: Utilization of energy storage systems charged from grid in buildings and comparison with solar systems
publicationTitle: IET Conference on Power in Unity: a Whole System Approach
abstract: This study is motivated by the fact that a big portion of energy consumption between the hours of 17:00 and 22:00 when the global energy consumption reaches very high levels occurs at residential areas. The aim here is to discuss the applicability of energy storage systems in the multi-apartment complexes with energy management systems by providing experimental results. The results also include an economic comparison between solar systems and energy storage systems. Savings reflected on the monthly bills both from the solar energy and stored energy consumption based on various scenarios and the time for return of investment resulting from these savings are also provided. The findings point out that the energy storage systems can produce substantial amounts of savings both for the end users and the country overall by letting the apartments store the energy when it is cheaper during the day and use the stored energy when it is expensive.

articleTitle: Novel scheme for load shedding and identification of critical tie-lines in WAMS emergency control
publicationTitle: IET Conference on Power in Unity: a Whole System Approach
abstract: The paper attempts to discuss a novel emergency control scheme, at conditions of transient instabilities, using real time data from synchrophasors. The rotor instability prediction methods such as rotor angle algorithm and energy function method are discussed with applications in the prediction or detection phase and a new algorithm has been formulated to compute the amount of the load to be shed at the time of contingencies. The algorithm is also extended to find out the critical tie lines and the buses at which the load is to be shed. The proposed method is a distributive load shedding scheme and hence reduces the chances of over loading in the tie lines. The algorithm is tested with 39 bus New England system and the results are formulated and discussed.

articleTitle: An energy storage system for the scottish isle of Gigha
publicationTitle: IET Conference on Power in Unity: a Whole System Approach
abstract: The areas of the United Kingdom that are best suited to renewable energy generation tend to be away from population centres. Here, electricity networks increasingly find themselves having to limit renewable energy ambitions; often there is no simple solution. Given the long life of many network assets, change is either slow or expensive. The wholly community-owned Isle of Gigha in Scotland today finds its renewable energy ambitions limited in this manner. This case study sets out the rationale for an Energy Storage solution for this community that would enable increased renewable energy capacity, yield and value; with the potential to explore many of the other benefits cases attributable to Energy Storage at the weak edge of the electricity network. In March 2013 this project was awarded Feasibility Stage funding under the Department for Energy and Climate Change's Energy Storage Demonstration Programme [1].
